examples.title: Coffee roaster in Austin, Texas
examples.subtitle: Sells 12 oz bags to cafés and grocers; tariffs on Brazilian beans are in the news
examples.text: I run a small specialty coffee roastery in Austin, Texas, buying green beans from Brazil and selling 12 oz bags to about 45 local cafés and grocers, around 300 bags a week. A bag sells for $13 wholesale and the beans, roasting and packaging cost me about $7.80. Beans take about 5 weeks to arrive by sea; I keep about 3 weeks of stock and could put about $12,000 into more. My main rival, Capital City Coffee, charges $12.50 a bag.

search_terms: tariff Brazil coffee imports US roasters
market_terms: new coffee chain opening Austin Texas

examples.title: Coffee roaster in Ho Chi Minh City
examples.subtitle: Sells robusta to cafés; bean prices are jumping
examples.text: I roast robusta in Ho Chi Minh City and sell 1 kg bags to about 60 independent cafés, around 280 bags a week. A bag sells for $11 and the green beans plus packaging cost me about $6.50. Beans from the Central Highlands take about 3 weeks to arrive; I keep about 2 weeks of stock and could put about $8,000 into more. My main rival is Highland Supply, who charge $10.50 a bag.

market_terms: chuỗi cà phê mới khai trương TP.HCM

examples.title: Online PC-parts shop
examples.subtitle: Imports graphics cards; new tariffs are in the news
examples.text: I run a small online shop in Hanoi that imports graphics cards from Taiwan for gamers and small studios. A mid-range card sells for $420 and costs me about $330 landed, and I sell around 90 a week. Orders from my distributor take about 4 weeks to arrive and I keep roughly 3 weeks of stock, with about $40,000 spare for more. My main rival, TechNova, sells the same card for $415.

examples.title: Furniture maker shipping to Europe
examples.subtitle: Ships from Bình Dương; Red Sea delays are in the news
examples.text: We make solid-wood dining sets in Bình Dương and ship them by sea to furniture retailers in Germany and the Netherlands. A set sells for about €900 and costs us about €560 in wood, hardware and finishing, and we sell around 40 a week. Shipping takes about 5 weeks door to door and we keep about 2 weeks of timber on hand. Our main rival, Baltic Woodworks, sells a similar set for €880.

memo.cost_line: Beans +30% × 60% of your cost is green beans = your cost +18% (+$1.40 a bag)

script.mode_reason: Offline demo: the recorded Austin coffee example is playing.
script.scenario_thought: Beans +30% is the news column. Two bigger worries for a small Austin roaster: the tariff could widen and Gulf port delays could push beans to +45% with slower shipping, and Capital City has said it will hold its prices, so a 5% cut is realistic. A regional chain with 25 new locations could pull 8% of your accounts. One column for a price fall, marked unlikely.
scenario_reasoning:
news n1: Brazil tariff, green coffee +30%. your beans = 60% of cost → cost +18%
7.80 × 0.60 × 0.30 = $1.40 a bag. margin 13.00 − 7.80 = $5.20 → 5.20 − 1.40 = $3.80
n2: Gulf port delays, +1 wk transit → could extend the spike. try +45%, shipping +2 wk
m2: Capital City 'will not pass it all on' → rival price −5% is plausible
m1: 25-location chain, own roasting → share shift ~8% of accounts from wk 4
also one downside column: beans −12%, unlikely but plans must not rely on a spike

unmodelled.text: A possible Texas sales-tax change on packaged coffee is being discussed
Larger grocers may ask for longer payment terms when prices rise

1:
seed results: stock 4 wk covers the spike but ties up a lot of cash
price +4% alone: little cash, fine in the news column, loses if beans fall back
try: stock 3 wk + raise 3% wk 3 → less cash, keeps the volume
try: stock 6 wk → big gain but cash > $12,000 → will show 'Over your cash'
2:
best so far: stock 3 wk + raise 3% wk 3. more stock helps while cash allows
stock 4 wk fits the $12,000 → combine with +3% wk 3
marketing +20% costs money now and brings little back → test it once

rounds.think: Starting with three simple plans: buy more stock, raise the price, or switch supplier.
rounds.test: Testing 3 starter plans against {n_shocks} futures, 1,000 runs per cell.
rounds.shoppers: Asked the shopper groups how each starter plan feels to them.

rounds.think: Stock helps but cash is tight. Trying a smaller stock-up with a price rise, and a bigger one.
rounds.test: Testing 2 new plans against all futures.
rounds.shoppers: Shoppers: price-hunters switch to Capital City faster than loyal buyers.

rounds.think: Combining what worked: 4 weeks of stock fits your cash, plus a small rise. One marketing test.
rounds.shoppers: Shoppers: a small rise after a stock-up reads as fair when everyone's costs jump.
